note: First half of the established-knowledge-lane landing. An external prototype (built in another session, forwarded as a full four-file paste) currently monkeypatches nestor.cascade.translate_segment to insert a recognition step between the tier-1 sealed lookup and the tier-2 engine call — a lexicon hit for `42`, a Jeles corpus hit for `What does HTTP 404 mean?`, etc. — landing them as drafts with citation warrants so a human does not have to pair what is culturally already paired. This decision adds the seam the prototype should register through, so a landing PR that follows can plug in cleanly instead of shipping a monkeypatch. Second half (nestor/established/) is a follow-up.

decisions.question: Should cascade.translate_segment expose a hook for tier-1.5 recognition (between the sealed lookup and the engine call)?
decisions.commitment: Yes. `nestor/cascade.py` adds a module-level `_tier15_recognizer` (nullable) with `set_tier15_recognizer(fn)` / `get_tier15_recognizer()` accessors and a private `_run_tier15_recognizer` that enforces the return contract. `translate_segment` calls the recognizer in an `elif` between the tier-1 hit branch and the tier-2 engine branch: sealed hit still short-circuits (recognizer is never asked about a sealed row), a recognizer that returns None falls through to the engine, and a recognizer that returns a Passage is served as-is with the ordinary passage entry appended to the ledger. Gated by 10 tests in tests/test_cascade_tier15_hook.py: no-recognizer path unchanged; sealed-still-wins (recognizer never called on tier-1 hit); returning None falls through; returning a draft Passage is served verbatim; recognizer receives (text, source_lang, target_lang, store, matcher); set(None) unregisters cleanly; second install replaces first; and ledger integration (a tier-1.5 draft lands under kind='passage' with engine/tier/state/confidence recorded).
decisions.why: The alternative — every consumer monkeypatching cascade.translate_segment — is what the forwarded prototype does today, and the prototype's own §8.1 names the monkeypatch as the thing to replace. A patch that duplicates tier-1 and tier-2 handling has to be kept in sync with every future cascade change (the monkeypatch runs its own memory.best_sealed call, its own engine.translate branch, its own document/segment queueing — three duplicated code paths, each a place the patch and the cascade can drift). A hook seam keeps the cascade in charge of tier 1 and tier 2 and lets the recognizer contribute exactly the tier-1.5 step it wants. The pattern matches how storage and matcher are already injected (`get_store(store)`, `matcher: Matcher | None = None`) — inject the seam once, unchanged callers get the pre-0205 shape, opt-in callers register through it.

decisions.question: What is the return contract, and what does the seam refuse?
decisions.commitment: The recognizer is `Callable[..., Passage | None]` — signature `(text, source_lang, target_lang, *, store, matcher) -> Passage | None`. Returning `None` falls through to the tier-2 engine unchanged. Returning a Passage is served as-is with two enforced refusals: (a) the returned Passage must be an actual `Passage` instance (a dict or other duck-type raises TypeError); (b) the returned Passage must not have `state='sealed'` (raises RuntimeError with the message 'the seam exists specifically to keep the sealed lane under the covenant's control at tier 1'). Both refusals happen inside `_run_tier15_recognizer` before the cascade appends anything to the ledger, so a bad recognizer produces an exception, not a laundered row.
decisions.why: The seal covenant is the tree's whole load-bearing rule ('You may propose. You may not confirm'). A recognizer that returned state='sealed' would be a fourth way to produce a serve-as-verified row without a human signing in nestor.ui — the three existing paths (memory.add_pair, cascade.translate_segment via tier-1 memory.best_sealed with valid signature, and portable.import_bundle with valid signature) are gated by the seal-signature verify; a recognizer callback is code the host wrote, not a signature check, and letting it produce sealed rows would collapse the whole distinction the covenant makes between authored-by-a-human and vouched-by-a-key. Refusing at the seam is a bright line, easy to hold, and impossible to circumvent by mistake.

decisions.question: Single recognizer or list-of-recognizers?
decisions.commitment: Single, for now. `set_tier15_recognizer(fn)` replaces the previously-installed one (no warning — a host installing twice deliberately is not doing it by mistake). If a second lane ever needs to co-exist (a lexicon AND a corpus AND a house-style TM, all wanting to be consulted before the engine), a wider design would move to `register_tier15_recognizer(fn)` / `unregister_tier15_recognizer(fn)` returning a token, with the cascade iterating the registered set and taking the first non-None. That design is named here so a later decision doesn't have to re-derive it.
decisions.why: The seat rule: 'Don't add features, refactor, or introduce abstractions beyond what the task requires. Three similar lines is better than a premature abstraction.' The one identified consumer (the established-knowledge lane) has a single recognizer that consults a lexicon first and jeles second internally — the two-source composition happens inside the recognizer, not across two hook-registered recognizers. Building the list variant now would ship API surface no caller uses; naming it as the wider design keeps the door open without paying for it today. The `set_*` shape stays a shape a `register_*` variant can subsume (`set_tier15_recognizer(x)` == `unregister_all(); register(x)`).

decisions.question: Why land the seam alone (this PR) before the established-lane module?
decisions.commitment: Reviewability. The seam is one file's edit (nestor/cascade.py) plus one test file (tests/test_cascade_tier15_hook.py) plus this decision — small enough that a reviewer can hold the whole change in one sitting and audit the covenant boundary. The established-knowledge lane the seam exists to host is a four-file module (lexicon, jeles bridge, wire, __init__), touches the warrant and evidence recipes, and needs its own tests over the lexicon and jeles integration; landing it in the same PR would mix two concerns whose blast radii are very different. This PR ships the seam; a follow-up PR ships `nestor/established/` registered through the seam.
decisions.why: The same seat rule applied to PR ordering: small, testable, one-concern-at-a-time. The seam is Nestor product surface (the covenant boundary lives here); the established-lane is a package that USES the surface. Splitting keeps the diffs proportional to the concerns, and lets each land or roll back independently. A revert on the seam PR breaks the established-lane's registration but not anything else; a revert on the established-lane PR takes the module out without touching the cascade.
